newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX gasoline ends up on strong cash market.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX gasoline ends up on strong cash market.

text.p: NYMEX gasoline prices ended higher Tuesday on the back of firm cash values in the U.S. Gulf while gasoline demand gathered pace abroad.
"Gasoline in the (U.S.) Gulf and Midcontinent have risen while there are plenty of stories about Nigeria needing gasoline," said Warren Tashnek, president of Fimat USA Futures in Houston.
May gasoline settled up 0.45 cent a gallon at 61.17 cents. May heating oil ended off 0.23 cent a gallon at 52.89 cents while May crude finished up 12 cents a barrel at $19.35.
Nigeria, a member of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, has been suffering from a two-week-old petrol shortage.
An official of the state-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) said Monday that the military government had given the green light for the first petrol imports since September.
Fuel shortages occur frequently in Nigeria and usually last a few days but the current crisis shows no sign of easing.
Meanwhile, traders said Saudi Arabia is looking to buy some 300,000 barrels of gasoline for delivery in early May.
European gasoline players said they expected the product to be supplied out of the Far or Middle East.
In the United States, gasoline has been firm in the U.S. Gulf cash market following a shipping deadline on the Houston end of the Colonial Pipeline which sends gasoline to the New York Harbor.
The Houston-to-New York Colonial Pipeline is the largest refined products pipeline in America, pumping nearly 20 percent of total daily U.S. refined products demand.
Dealers also noted some position squaring ahead of weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) expected Tuesday evening.
After the market closed, the API released a report that fell within expectations for both crude and refined products.

It said gasoline stocks fell 1.22 million barrels while crude stocks rose 1.05 million barrels for the week ended April 4. Distillate stocks, which reflect heating oil and diesel, dropped 1.04 million barrels.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
